items.title: Single Number II
items.statement: Implement ones/twos; then column-counting alternative aloud.

solutionCode.label: two-register mod-3 automaton, plus the general column count
solutionCode.py:
def single_number_ii(a: list) -> int:
    """Two-register mod-3 automaton. Per bit position:
         (ones, twos) = (0,0) seen 0 times, (1,0) once, (0,1) twice.
       A third occurrence returns the pair to (0,0)."""
    ones = twos = 0
    for x in a:
        x &= 0xFFFFFFFF
        ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos & 0xFFFFFFFF
        twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return ones - (1 << 32) if ones >> 31 else ones     # back to signed


def single_number_mod_k(a: list, k: int) -> int:
    """GENERAL k: count set bits per column mod k. O(32n), any k."""
    result = 0
    for bit in range(32):
        count = sum((x >> bit) & 1 for x in a)
        if count % k:
            result |= 1 << bit          # this column belongs to the loner
    return result - (1 << 32) if result >> 31 else result

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1). The column-counting alternative is O(32n) time and O(1) space, and generalises to any k.

followups.q: Trace one bit position through three occurrences.
followups.a: Start (ones,twos) = (0,0). First x with that bit set: ones becomes 1, twos stays 0 (since ~ones is now 0 at that position). Second: ones ^ 1 is 0, so ones becomes 0; twos ^ 1 is 1 and ~ones is 1, so twos becomes 1. Third: ones ^ 1 is 1 but ~twos is 0, so ones stays 0; twos ^ 1 is 0, so twos becomes 0. Back to (0,0) after exactly three — the counter is mod 3.

followups.q: Which version would you write under pressure?
followups.a: The column count. It is obviously correct, generalises to any k with a one-character change, and costs O(32n) which is fine at n = 3*10^4. The two-register automaton is O(n) with a tiny constant but is easy to get subtly wrong in the ordering of the two assignments — write it only if you can derive it live.

items.title: Sum of Two Integers
hints: Section trace your own pair e.g. -7+3.

solutionCode.label: half adder: XOR is the sum without carry, AND shifted is the carry
solutionCode.py:
MASK32 = 0xFFFFFFFF


def get_sum(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Half adder: XOR is the sum without carry, (AND << 1) is the carry.
    Python has unbounded ints, so mask to 32 bits to mimic C++ wraparound."""
    x, y = a & MASK32, b & MASK32
    while y:
        carry = ((x & y) << 1) & MASK32   # where BOTH have a 1, carry left
        x = (x ^ y) & MASK32              # sum ignoring carries
        y = carry                          # fold the carry back in
    return x - (1 << 32) if x >> 31 else x    # reinterpret as signed

items.complexity: O(width) — at most 32 carry-propagation rounds. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why must this be done in unsigned?
followups.a: Carry propagation routinely overflows the value range mid-computation, and signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C++ — the compiler may assume it never happens and optimise the loop away. Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap, which is exactly the two's-complement behaviour the algorithm relies on.

followups.q: Why does this work for negative numbers with no sign handling?
followups.a: Two's complement makes addition sign-agnostic: the same bit pattern operations produce the correct result whether the operands are read as signed or unsigned. That is the entire point of the representation, and it is why the trace of -7 + 3 needs no special case.

items.title: Divide Two Integers

solutionCode.label: long division by repeated doubling, with the INT_MIN / -1 clamp
solutionCode.py:
INT_MAX, INT_MIN = 2**31 - 1, -2**31


def divide(dividend: int, divisor: int) -> int:
    """Long division by repeated doubling, no * / % anywhere."""
    # THE ONLY OVERFLOW CASE: INT_MIN / -1 is 2**31, which does not fit.
    if dividend == INT_MIN and divisor == -1:
        return INT_MAX

    negative = (dividend < 0) != (divisor < 0)     # sign extracted FIRST
    a, b = abs(dividend), abs(divisor)

    quotient = 0
    for shift in range(31, -1, -1):
        # if b fits into the remaining dividend when scaled by 2^shift, take it
        if (a >> shift) >= b:
            a -= b << shift
            quotient |= 1 << shift
    return -quotient if negative else quotient

items.complexity: O(log^2 n) with the doubling search — 32 outer iterations each doing up to 32 shifts. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is INT_MIN / -1 the only overflow case?
followups.a: Division shrinks magnitude except when dividing the most negative value by -1: |INT_MIN| is 2^31, one larger than INT_MAX. Every other quotient fits. The problem specifies clamping to INT_MAX, so it is a single explicit guard rather than a class of cases.

Negating INT_MIN as a signed int is undefined behaviour — the positive value has no representation. Casting to unsigned first gives 2147483648 correctly, since unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap. Writing abs(dividend) on INT_MIN is the classic bug this problem hides.

items.title: Reverse Bits
items.statement: Both loop-reverse AND 5-round butterfly; compare cycles.
hints: Read hex masks as binary block patterns.

solutionCode.label: bit-by-bit loop, then the 5-round butterfly swap
solutionCode.py:
MASK32 = 0xFFFFFFFF


def reverse_bits_loop(n: int) -> int:
    """Pull bits off the bottom, push them onto the top."""
    n &= MASK32
    out = 0
    for _ in range(32):
        out = ((out << 1) | (n & 1)) & MASK32
        n >>= 1
    return out


def reverse_bits_butterfly(n: int) -> int:
    """Swap adjacent blocks of size 1, then 2, 4, 8, 16.
    Read the hex masks as block patterns:
      0x55555555 = 0101...  single bits
      0x33333333 = 0011...  pairs
      0x0F0F0F0F = nibbles
      0x00FF00FF = bytes"""
    n &= MASK32
    n = ((n >> 1) & 0x55555555) | ((n & 0x55555555) << 1)
    n = ((n >> 2) & 0x33333333) | ((n & 0x33333333) << 2)
    n = ((n >> 4) & 0x0F0F0F0F) | ((n & 0x0F0F0F0F) << 4)
    n = ((n >> 8) & 0x00FF00FF) | ((n & 0x00FF00FF) << 8)
    n = ((n >> 16) | (n << 16)) & MASK32
    return n
# CYCLES: the loop is 32 dependent iterations; the butterfly is 5 independent
# rounds of three operations. On a real CPU the butterfly wins by 5-10x.

items.complexity: Loop version O(32). Butterfly version is 5 rounds of shift-mask-or — constant with no data dependence on the input.

followups.q: Explain the butterfly in one sentence.
followups.a: Reversing a sequence equals recursively swapping its two halves and reversing each half — done bottom-up, that is: swap adjacent bits, then adjacent pairs, then nibbles, bytes, and finally halves. Five rounds because 2^5 = 32.

followups.q: Why does each round need two masks?
followups.a: One extracts the bits moving right and one the bits moving left, so they can be shifted in opposite directions and OR-ed without colliding. Using a single mask would leave the other half's bits in place and corrupt the result — the mask and its complement are doing symmetric halves of one swap.

items.title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
items.statement: O(31) solution + brute-force explanation why it TLEs.

solutionCode.label: the answer is the common binary prefix of m and n
solutionCode.py:
def range_bitwise_and(m: int, n: int) -> int:
    shifts = 0
    while m < n:
        m >>= 1
        n >>= 1
        shifts += 1                 # strip differing low bits
    return m << shifts              # restore with zeros below
# WHY: if m < n then some bit flips across the range, and every column below the
# highest differing position takes both values -- so each contains a 0 and ANDs
# to 0. Only the shared high prefix survives.
# BRUTE FORCE dies because the range can span 2^31 values.

items.complexity: O(32) — one shift per bit at worst. The brute force is O(n - m), which is up to 2^31 iterations and always times out.

followups.q: Why does every bit below the differing position AND to zero?
followups.a: If m and n differ at some bit position p, the range crosses a value where bit p flips. Crossing that boundary forces all bits below p through a full 0-to-1 cycle, so each of those columns contains at least one 0 somewhere in the range. A single 0 in a column makes the whole AND 0 there.

followups.q: Why exactly does the brute force TLE?
followups.a: The constraint allows 0 <= m <= n <= 2^31 - 1, so the range can hold over two billion values. Even at a billion ANDs per second that is seconds per query, versus the 31 shifts the prefix method needs. It is not a constant-factor problem — it is the wrong algorithm.

items.title: Subsets — bitmask edition
items.statement: Same output as R201 but pure-mask implementation; discuss when masks beat recursion.
hints: Order differs from recursion's — note it.

solutionCode.label: each mask IS a subset; bit j means "take a[j]"
solutionCode.py:
def subsets_mask(a: list) -> list:
    """Each mask IS a subset: bit j means 'take a[j]'.

    ORDER DIFFERS from the recursive pick/not-pick version -- masks ascend
    numerically, so [] comes first, then [a0], [a1], [a0,a1], ...
    The SET of subsets is identical; the sequence is not."""
    n = len(a)
    return [[a[j] for j in range(n) if mask & (1 << j)]
            for mask in range(1 << n)]

items.complexity: Time O(n * 2^n) to build all subsets, same as the recursion. Space O(1) beyond the output — no call stack at all.

followups.a: When you need to INDEX subsets — bitmask DP keyed on "which items are used" requires the mask as a memo key anyway, so generating them directly avoids a translation layer. Masks also have no call-stack cost and are trivially parallelisable, since each mask is independent. Recursion wins when you need pruning, because a mask loop cannot skip a subtree.

followups.q: What is the hard limit on this approach?
followups.a: n must be under about 25 — 2^25 is 33 million subsets. Beyond that both time and memory explode regardless of implementation. If n exceeds roughly 20 and you still need subsets, the problem almost certainly wants DP over masks rather than enumeration of them.
